opus-5.5.text:
I think it started pretty simply, honestly. The first year, I went to Husha almost on a whim. A few friends and I had this idea that we could do something useful over the summer, and a volunteer teaching camp seemed like a natural fit. We didn't have a grand plan. We just wanted to spend a few weeks with the kids there and teach them some things they might not get in their regular classes: some science, some English, a bit about the world outside the village.

But what surprised me was how much that first summer stayed with me afterward. You go in thinking you're the one giving something, and then you realize the kids are giving you just as much, maybe more. Their curiosity, the way they'd ask questions that I had never thought to ask myself. And at the end of the camp, when we were leaving, some of them asked, "Will you come back next year?" That question was hard to walk away from.

So the second year was partly a promise. I felt that if we only came once, it would be a nice memory for them, but it wouldn't really change much. Continuity matters. The kids remember you, you remember them, and you can actually see them grow. A child who was shy the first year starts raising their hand the second year. By the third year, some of the older ones were almost helping us run activities. That kind of change only shows up if you keep showing up.

And there was a more personal reason too. Running the camp forced me to think about what I actually care about. In school, or in research, a lot of what you do is abstract, and the feedback loop is long. In Husha, the feedback is immediate. You see whether a lesson works on a kid's face. That kept me grounded. It reminded me that education, at its core, is about people, about opening a door for someone, even a little bit.

By the third year, it didn't feel like a decision anymore. It just felt like part of my summer, part of who I was. And I think we also got better at it. We learned what the kids actually needed rather than what we assumed they needed. That learning process, getting a little less naive each year, was meaningful in itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first year I didn't plan on going back. I thought of it as a one-off thing, a summer, a stamp on a resume if I'm being blunt. But what happened at the end of that first camp is that the kids asked whether we'd come again next year, and I said yes without really thinking about it. And then it became a question of whether I was the kind of person who meant what he said to a nine-year-old.

The second year is actually the hardest one. The novelty is gone, you know exactly how tired you'll be, the fundraising is harder because people already gave once. But that's also the year you start to see something. Kids who wouldn't speak in the first summer were standing up to read in front of the class. One girl remembered a chemistry experiment we did, down to the smell. That told me the thing wasn't just entertainment for them, it was actually sticking.

And by the third year it stopped feeling like "my project." The villagers started preparing the classroom before we arrived, a few older students were helping teach the younger ones. At that point you're not deciding whether to keep running it, you're just deciding whether to show up to something that already exists. So I'd say what kept me going was less a grand motivation and more a kind of obligation that turned into affection. Husha became a place I belong to a little, not a place I visit.
